name: Maratino
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Estado general de las fundaciones hechas por D. José de Escandón en la colonia del Nuevo Santander.. y un apéndice con la Relación histórica del Nuevo Santander por Fr. Vicente Santa María. 1929-30. México: Archivo General de la Nación (Publicaciones XIV-XV), vol. 1.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Vol. 1 scanned searched for maratin/chiguat/nighua/hebreo/acento: the linguistic passage and song are not in this volume (only 'las flechas de los maratines' in the editor's introduction, line 648).

sources.citation: Stresser-Péan, Guy. 2000. San Antonio Nogalar: la Sierra de Tamaulipas y la frontera noreste de Mesoamérica. México: CEMCA. Cap. 8 'Tribus semiagrícolas del contorno de la sierra de Tamaulipas y de la región de Aldama' (OpenEdition Books, doi:10.4000/books.cemca.6748).
sources.note: Nothing; the Maratines are treated only geographically (Sierra de San José de las Rusias / sierra de los maratines, paras. 5-6).

sources.citation: Campbell, Lyle. 1997. American Indian Languages: The Historical Linguistics of Native America. New York: OUP. Section 1.14.2 'Maratino' (p. 948 in the offprint pagination of the balsas-nahuatl.org scan).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Only classification: Swanton 1940:122-4 published the scant material; Swadesh 1963, 1968 called it Tamaulipeco or Maratín and put it in Uto-Aztecan; 'I find little to recommend this' (chiguat and peyot are Nahuatl loans).

sources.citation: Swadesh, Mauricio. 1968. Las lenguas indígenas del noreste de México. Anales de Antropología 5(1).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative/historical survey; Swadesh's second treatment of Tamaulipeco/Maratín; open access at UNAM but the OJS site is behind an automated-access block by automated download.

sources.citation: Swanton, John R. 1940. Linguistic material from the tribes of southern Texas and northeastern Mexico. Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 127. Washington: GPO. Maratino-English vocabulary 'from the Spanish of Father Santa Maria', pp. 122-124; phonetic remarks pp. 5, 8-10.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Maratino stress. p. 10 says the recording symbols for 'San Francisco Solano and Maratino, could not be otherwise than defective'; the only accent sentence ('The accents in Comecrudo, Cotoname, and the Karankawa recorded by Dr. Gatschet are as given by the last named investigator') excludes Maratino. The vocabulary keeps a few of Santa Maria's acute accents (memehé, maamehé, tutcé) but states no rule.

sources.citation: Pimentel, Francisco. 1903-04 [1874-75]. Obras completas (Cuadro descriptivo y comparativo de las lenguas indígenas de México, vol. III), appendix pp. 493-496: 'breve relación sobre el idioma Maratin de Tamaulipas (extinguido según el P. Santa María)' and 'Canto de los maratines traducido por el P. Santa María'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Re-copies the same Santa María passage and song (same acute accents); no accent or stress statement.

sources.citation: Prieto, Alejandro. 1873. Historia, geografía y estadística del Estado de Tamaulipas. México: Tip. Escalerillas. pp. 117-120 (quoting Fray Vicente de Santa María's Relación histórica de la colonia del Nuevo Santander, c. 1790s).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Santa María's remarks cover verb inflection, noun plurals by vowel lengthening (chiguat / chiguata / aachiguata 'prolongando mas y mas las A. A.') and the simile particle nighua; nothing on accent. The 12-line song is printed with Spanish acute accents on many word-final syllables (catamá, memehé, maamehé, coomutepá, tzemahká, Chenohgimá, mohká, hemigtuché) and none elsewhere -- raw orthographic marks, no statement.

sources.citation: Zamponi, Raoul. 2024. Extinct lineages and unclassified languages of Mexico. In Carolyn J. MacKay & Frank R. Trechsel (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mexico and Northern Central America, 99-158. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

sources.note: The primary manuscript source of every Maratino form; a modern edition may reproduce Santa María's own accent marks more faithfully than Prieto 1873 / Swanton 1940 and may contain remarks omitted by Prieto. The 1929 AGN edition vol. 1 (on archive.org) does not contain the language passage.

sources.note: The only dedicated linguistic analysis of the Maratino/Tamaulipeco corpus (cited by Campbell 1997 as the source of the Uto-Aztecan proposal); a re-phonemicization of Santa María's text might comment on the accent marks. Not online (RMEA vol. 19 not on archive.org; only vol. 17 (1961) found).

Indian languages of Mexico and Central America and their geographical distribution. BAE Bulletin 44 (overview; 'Tamaulipeco = Maratino').
